title: Uncertainty-aware evidential learning for legal case retrieval with noisy correspondence
abstract: Legal case retrieval is a critical task in intelligent legal systems, providing relevant precedents to assist judges in their decision-making. While current data-driven neural retrieval methods have demonstrated impressive performance on clean, annotated data, they often ignore the robustness against noisy correspondences. In practice, legal annotators are required to identify legal uncertainty, which refers to the ambiguity or unpredictability in legal interpretations and applications, in relevance estimation between cases. This uncertainty often introduces noise into the training data, leading to unreliable predictions and potentially impacting the fairness and justice of downstream tasks. Focusing on this robustness issue, we propose a novel evidential learning framework called ELCR, which explicitly models the legal uncertainty and addresses noisy correspondences. Specifically, we first estimate the multi-faceted relevance between query-candidate cases from the concept, rule, and fact levels. These relevance estimations are then used to obtain the evidence-based uncertainty under the Dempster-Shafer Evidence Theory, which helps correct labels from noisy correspondence. Guided by two elaborate evidence-based training objectives, ELCR provides accurate uncertainty estimation, enhancing reliability and robustness. Extensive experiments on various noise proportions across two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method exhibits robustness against noisy correspondences while maintaining competitive retrieval performance.
research_problem: Existing neural legal case retrieval methods rely on clean annotated data and overlook robustness against noisy correspondences caused by legal uncertainty (ambiguity at the concept, rule, and fact levels), leading to unreliable predictions and limiting practical application.
methodology: Proposes ELCR, an evidential learning framework that estimates multi-faceted query-candidate relevance from concept, rule, and fact levels; parameterizes relevance evidence into a Dirichlet distribution under Dempster-Shafer Evidence Theory to quantify uncertainty; corrects noisy labels via an uncertainty-based strategy with warm-up stabilization; and optimizes with standard relevance loss plus two evidence-based objectives.

methods.name: Multi-faceted relevance modeling
methods.description: Estimates relevance from neural semantic, concept-level, law-level, and fact-level modules using sentence-concept/law/fact similarity aggregation and a linear fusion layer.

methods.name: Evidential uncertainty estimation
methods.description: Parameterizes relevance evidence into a Dirichlet distribution using Dempster-Shafer Evidence Theory to compute belief masses and an uncertainty mass for each query-candidate pair.

methods.name: Label correction strategy
methods.description: Corrects observed labels with high uncertainty based on relevance evidence, using a warm-up phase and a stabilization threshold to prevent over-correction and training fluctuation.

methods.name: Evidence-based contrastive learning
methods.description: Minimizes the expected squared error between predicted Dirichlet probabilities and corrected labels to generate more evidence for correct predictions and reduce variance.

methods.name: Uncertainty penalty loss
methods.description: Applies a KL divergence regularization term between the predictive Dirichlet distribution and a uniform Dirichlet to penalize divergences from uncertain retrievals.

methods.name: Criminal-BERT backbone
methods.description: Implements the neural relevance module using Criminal-BERT; the framework is model-agnostic and also compatible with BERT and Lawformer.

datasets.name: LeCaRD
datasets.description: Legal case retrieval dataset for the Chinese law system with 107 queries and 100 candidate cases per query.

datasets.name: ELAM
datasets.description: Legal case retrieval dataset with 85 queries and 50 candidate cases per query.

contributions: First evidential learning framework (ELCR) to explicitly model multi-faceted relevance uncertainties and detect noisy correspondences in legal case retrieval.
Uncertainty-based label correction strategy with warm-up and stabilization mechanisms to prevent over-correction during training.
Two uncertainty-based learning objectives—evidence-based contrastive loss and uncertainty penalty loss—to ensure a desired evidence distribution.
Demonstrated robustness against various noise proportions (10%–90%) while maintaining competitive retrieval performance.
findings: ELCR exhibits robustness against noisy correspondences while maintaining competitive retrieval performance across benchmark datasets.
Achieves average NDCG improvements of 20.90% on LeCaRD and 10.99% on ELAM compared to various baselines.
Explicit modeling of legal uncertainty via evidential learning improves reliability and enables effective noise identification.
Framework is adaptable across different backbone architectures, including BERT, Criminal-BERT, and Lawformer.
limitations: In high-noise scenarios, imperfect differentiation between noisy positive samples and true negatives may reduce the number of available positive samples and degrade performance.
Additional computational overhead from evidence calculation, uncertainty estimation, and label correction may challenge resource-constrained environments.
